1:
What it is to enter into the congregation of the Lord is disputed, and Henry lays out three readings without settling on one. Some take it of communicating with the people of God in religious service, so that though such men were owned as members, and Ammonites and Moabites might be proselyted, they must lie for a time under marks of disgrace and not come so near the sanctuary as others. Some take it of bearing office, none being eligible as elder or judge, lest the honour of the magistracy be stained. Some take it only of marrying with Israelites, as Bishop Patrick inclines. Clarke chooses the second and gives its reason plainly: no man with a defect that might make him contemptible should bear rule, lest the contempt felt for his person be transferred to his office; the general sense is that such persons were not to be so incorporated with the Jews as to share their civil privileges. Wesley agrees, arguing from the word itself, which generally means a company met together; since the whole body of the people could never assemble in one place, the term must here denote the rulers who frequently did. He adds that eunuchs were commonly observed to want the courage a governor needs, and being despised would expose their authority to the same contempt.

Calvin will have none of this. Both the office reading and the marriage reading he calls tame: what is afterwards said of certain foreign nations cannot be taken as merely barring them from dignity, and the phrase congregation of the Lord sufficiently expresses the purity and holiness of religion. He does not doubt that those defiled by these two stains are forbidden to communicate in the sacrifices. Though circumcised like the rest, God would have them bear this mark of disgrace as an example, so the people might be the more diligent in preserving themselves from pollution; the privilege denied them was that peculiar to legitimate Israelites, of entering the court to perform solemn service. On the physical definition Calvin thinks the Jews dispute more curiously than the subject warrants: God intended only to exclude the mutilated wherever holy assemblies were held, and the word takes in more cases than are specified. Gill notes that the injury is purposed and not accidental, inflicted to make the man unfit for generation; Keil renders the Hebrew literally as wounded by crushing.

Keil sets the chapter in order: from the sanctifying of the house, which the previous laws of marriage touched, Moses turns to the sanctifying of the people's union as a congregation — who is shut out and who received, the purity of the camp in war, foreign slaves and the removal of the licentious, and last certain duties of citizenship. Against the apparent harshness both Henry and Ellicott set the same counterweight. Ellicott thinks the rule was meant to keep Israelitish rulers from making eunuchs of their brethren, and points to the promise that those who keep God's sabbaths shall have within his house a place and a name better than of sons and daughters; Henry makes the same use of it, that though they seemed cast out of the vineyard as dry trees, the want of this privilege should be made up with blessings entitling them to that name. He adds that it was foretold to Hezekiah as a calamity that his descendants should be eunuchs in Babylon, though Daniel and his companions have ennobled that sort for ever; and we cannot tell whether those serving the kings of Israel were Israelites at all — Ebedmelech, at least, was a foreigner. He closes with a contrast: circumcision was the sign of the covenant, mutilation a form of heathen self-devotion — which gives Paul's sharp words to the Galatians a double edge, since by doing what he names they would cut themselves off from the congregation of the Lord.
2:
The word rendered bastard does not mean what an English reader assumes it does. Keil denies it covers illegitimate children generally, as the Greek and Latin versions took it, holding with the Talmud that it means those begotten in incest or adultery. Clarke says the same, and Gill reports the common Jewish reading, gathered from the fact that this law follows on the incests forbidden at the close of the preceding chapter. Calvin distinguishes further. All agree it means one born of an uncertain father, but some extend it to every child of fornication while others confine it to those whose mothers, by gross prostitution, had made their children a monstrous medley; the second opinion he approves. What he will not allow is that the shame falls on the child as guilt: God would not exclude these unhappy persons from the hope of salvation, though through no fault of their own they could not name a father, but humbled them by temporal punishment only. Keil sees the same purpose in the number: ten being the number of complete exclusion, the tenth generation does not preclude all possibility. Gill passes on the rabbinic view that the law was framed to deter, adulterers seeing they fix an irreparable stain on their family.

With Ammon and Moab the ground shifts, and Calvin says so: it is foolish to attribute the sentence to their incestuous origin when another reason is plainly given. Keil agrees against Knobel — not because their forefathers were begotten in incest, but for the hostility they showed to God's kingdom: they failed to meet Israel with bread and water, and hired Balaam, drawing on themselves the curse that falls on all who curse Israel. Calvin presses the aggravation. They were descendants of Lot and should have embraced Abraham's children as brethren, so it was inexcusable barbarity to attack men who had offered peace and promised to pass quietly through. In hiring a mercenary to launch curses, he adds, they attempted to overwhelm God by magical incantations; nor did they err through ignorance, but persevered until Balaam was confounded from heaven — which shows what vengeance awaits those who of deliberate malice oppose God's grace. Gill and Ellicott both record the rabbinic limitation of the rule to men, an Ammonite and not an Ammonitess, the children following the father, which leaves Ruth untouched; Clarke observes the bar did not disqualify from proselytism, since she married Boaz and became a progenitor of our Lord.

Edom and Egypt are treated gently, and Calvin thinks the leniency itself part of the sentence on Moab: those two were manifestly dishonoured for their guilt, when not even aliens were dealt with so. Yet the inequality troubles him. Edom appeared in arms before Moab did and, being nearer of blood, was the less excusable. Calvin finds no reason except that God would show it depends on his own will to chastise the same sins more lightly in some than in others; since all deserve destruction, he justly keeps the free right of sparing whom he will, and we must adore judgments we cannot fathom. On Egypt he answers the objection of barbarous cruelty to fugitives who had trusted them by pointing to their first reception rather than their later tyranny: refugees were kindly received when Canaan was perishing of hunger. Wesley puts the lesson plainly: thou wast a stranger and didst receive habitation, protection and provision a long time, and that kindness must not be forgotten for the persecution that followed, since with men one injury blots out the remembrance of twenty courtesies, but God does not deal so with us. Ellicott adds a sharper contrast from Rashi: he who makes a man sin treats him worse than he who kills him — so Edom with the sword and Egypt with drowning are not to be abhorred, while those who counselled Israel into sin are.
9:
Henry reads the whole passage as one charge, and reduces it to a word: be clean. The camp is to be kept from three kinds of pollution, moral, ceremonial and natural, and the ninth verse covers the first. When the host goes out, every man is to look on himself as specially bound to keep from every evil thing. The soldiers must beware of sin, Henry says, because sin takes off the edge of valour and guilt makes men cowards; those who carry their lives in their hands need a conscience void of offence, that they may look death in the face without terror. They must not gratify malice, covetousness or uncleanness under cover of their commission, nor keep the accursed things they find in the camps they plunder. And the charge does not stop at the front. Those who stayed at home were bound by it too, lest their sin provoke God to withdraw from the army and give the victory to the enemy for the correction of his own people; times of war should be times of reformation, or how shall we expect an answer to our prayers for success? Wesley gives three reasons in a line: war is a season of confusion and licence, when the laws of God and man cannot be heard for the noise of arms; success depends on a blessing which wicked men have no reason to expect; and a man with his life in his hand had need be prepared for death and judgment.

Calvin takes the same verse as an argument against excuses. What had been taught about purity at home and in peace is here extended to the clang of arms. He observes how greatly laws are disregarded in war, when everything is under the control of violence rather than reason, and how much licence is granted to soldiers that would not be tolerated otherwise; God removes the plea by requiring the same purity in both conditions. This is not a special rule for the field, as though a man might sin freely at home — the general prohibition of impurity stands already — but a warning that the necessity of war will not be accepted as a defence. From which, Calvin concludes, we gather that empty excuses for violating God's commands are worthless in every case: however hard the duty, God never resigns his rights. Indeed the reasoning runs the other way. If war, which seems to suspend all law, does not excuse a crime, far heavier is the guilt of those who pollute themselves in peace, with quiet minds and nothing to hurry them.

The ceremonial and natural pollutions follow. Keil notes a tightening: in the desert march only lasting uncleannesses put a man outside the camp, but in an encampment even the lighter defilement of a night does, until he has washed at evening and the sun is down. Henry draws the moral, that the soldier is not discharged from the ceremony by his duties but bound more strictly — at home he need only wash, in the army he must withdraw, ashamed of his own impurity and concerned to keep the camp pure. Then the spade fastened to the weapon, and the covering of what passes from the bowels. Calvin knows the scoffers who think Moses ridiculous here, as though the smell offended the nostrils of God, and answers that these rudiments held the people to their duty, since licence in the smallest things leads on to audacity; nor was it merely sanitary, as others suppose. Clarke, more plainly, says decency and cleanliness promote health and prevent disease. Keil puts the point exactly: there was nothing shameful in the excrement, but the irreverence of leaving it would offend the Lord who walked in the midst, and drive him from the camp.
15:
Every commentator narrows the law before expounding it, since taken flat it makes Israel a refuge for every runaway. Gill supplies the missing clause: the servant meant is one used ill by a tyrannical master, in danger of his life or of being maimed, and driven to escape. Such a man is not bound and sent back, but kept until his master's anger subsides, or the quarrel inquired into and the two reconciled; if his flight proves just and return unsafe, he is settled as the next verse directs. It cannot be thought, Gill adds, that the law protects every idle and disobedient servant, which would be unjust. The Jewish writers, Onkelos with them, read it of servants of idolaters fleeing for religion's sake, and Clarke agrees: a servant who left an idolatrous master to join God's people — otherwise it would be injustice to harbour a runaway. Keil reads it of one fled from abroad because of harsh treatment by a heathen owner. Wesley argues from distance that the master must be a near neighbour, since a man would hardly flee so far, nor a master pursue so far; and it is not strange that the God who hates tyranny and calls himself the refuge of the oppressed should interpose to rescue such persons.

Calvin alone states the difficulty before answering it. The law tends to humanity, he grants, yet seems not altogether just. Elsewhere the remedy was milder: slaves might take sanctuary in temples, or at Rome at the statues of the Caesars, and on proving ill usage were sold to gentler owners — endurable enough. But the refuge granted here defrauds masters of their right, since without a hearing the fugitives may live in Canaan; the law of nations is violated, the land thrown open to every deserter; and because runaways are commonly criminal, their asylum fills with sources of infection. Suppose a thief or a murderer left his master for the Holy Land — sheltering such a guest would overthrow justice and set up a state of foul barbarism. Calvin therefore holds more is meant than the words express: if the man fled not for his own misdeeds but from excessive cruelty, the people were not to drive him out, which would be to give him up to butchery. That judicial proceedings were held he infers from the choice of city allowed him. Religion counted for something, since whoever sought a home there had to dedicate himself to God; but God would never let his name be profaned by receiving the wicked indiscriminately. So the law goes, in Calvin's arrangement, among the supplements of the sixth commandment: it forbids the people to become accessory to another's cruelty, the masters being in effect executioners, and provides for these wretched beings only so far as to let them plead their innocence in court.

Henry makes the land a sanctuary, a city of refuge for wronged servants from neighbouring countries, guarded by the same caution — Israel did not need, as Rome at first did, to be peopled by unprincipled men. The trembling servant is not handed to his enraged master until trial shows he wronged him and deserves punishment. It is honourable, Henry says, to shelter the weak if they are not wicked, and God allows his people to patronise the oppressed; the angel sent Hagar back and Paul Onesimus, neither having cause to leave nor danger in returning; but this man runs for his life, having heard Israel are a merciful people, and to give him up is to throw a lamb into the mouth of a lion. If the abuse is proved, protection is not enough: he must be encouraged to settle where it likes him best, neither imposed upon nor trading one hard master for many. Converts, Henry concludes, deserve particular tenderness, that they have no temptation to go back.
16:
Gill takes the provision for the fugitive's dwelling as confirming his reading — the law makes room for him among the Israelites, so he must be a proselyte servant, not any deserter. Keil sets the two rulings side by side as toleration and its refusal: the escaped slave may settle where he likes and must not be oppressed; but prostitutes of Israelite descent, male or female, were not to be endured at all. The point, Keil insists, is cultic: what was forbidden was that any Israelite should give himself up to prostitution as an act of worship. Foreign prostitutes were already excluded by the command to root out the Canaanites, and the two words used name those who prostituted themselves in the service of Astarte. Ellicott agrees in a line — both terms belong to the temples of Baal and Ashtaroth, persons dedicated to impurity. Gill dwells on the strangeness of the Hebrew, which properly means a holy one and here by contrary usage an impure one, defiled by man; Jarchi glosses it as a woman who separates herself for the trade and then makes herself common. Some restrict it to sacred harlots rather than street ones, and Gill cites Strabo on the temple of Venus at Corinth, so rich that above a thousand were kept there, devoted by men and women alike, with a like multitude at Comana, which Strabo calls little Corinth.

Calvin is less confident of the etymology. Some derive the word from being set apart for sin, but he thinks the pollution, as the opposite of holiness, better expressed otherwise; at any rate a precept of chastity is given, that unmarried girls should not have connection with men. The second clause he leaves open: elsewhere the masculine word plainly means a male harlot, but it may simply mean a fornicator, and he cites Job on hypocrites dying young with their life among such men, which amounts to calling their life infamous. If sodomy is preferred, Calvin adds, Leviticus condemns all such impurity anyway. Wesley reads a bar on the common prostitution the Gentiles tolerated and even used in worship — not that strangers among them were allowed it, but that it was forbidden to Israelites in a peculiar manner, as far more odious in them.

The wages are refused with the trade. Clarke observes that many public prostitutes dedicated part of their impure earnings to their gods, some being kept in the temple of Venus Melytta with their gains applied to that worship, and Wesley says the same, adding that the price of a dog means the whoremonger's takings, dogs being so called in the Revelation. Ellicott presses the words: even a lamb or kid might not be sacrificed if it came as the wages of sin, and while an ass could be redeemed with a lamb and the lamb offered, the dog admits no such exchange — the dogs may eat the children's crumbs, but there is also the dog that returns to his vomit, and without are dogs and sorcerers. Calvin notices an oddity: killing a pig was as wrong as killing a dog, yet a pig's price might be offered, so the dog is rejected not merely as unclean but as vile and contemptible, and the whole precept impresses the reverence due to the altar. Then usury. Gill and Wesley agree that the Israelite borrowed rarely, being a farmer and not a merchant, and only for subsistence or some emergency, so interest would have crushed him; the stranger lived by trade and gained by what he borrowed, and it is just the lender should share the gain. Calvin turns it into a positive duty: it is not enough to refrain from taking another's goods unless we also exercise mercy, since liberality is a part of righteousness, and he is unrighteous who will not relieve his brethren when he can.
21:
Calvin files vowing under the third commandment, since by it men train themselves in hallowing God's name, and to promise God anything is a kind of swearing. What between men is a covenant is, toward God, a vow — a sacred engagement not merely made with God as witness but contracted with him. The Nazarite's consecration he places under the first commandment instead. Here Moses confirms that God's name is not to be taken in vain, and commands payment, since withholding dims that name, defrauds God of his right and annuls a promise ratified before him. The vows that pleased God, Calvin adds, were testimonies of gratitude, a spur when the saints felt slow to proclaim his goodness; men in trouble bind themselves by a promise and must not cheat God once the danger is past, seeing with what levity many rush in and how lightly they break loose. Gill limits the matter to what is in a man's power, lawful, and agreeable to God's revealed will — a sacrifice beyond the required, a gift toward the sanctuary or the poor. Ellicott notes that Rashi and the rabbis make the three yearly feasts the occasions for payment, and that Ecclesiastes takes the precept up with enough difference to be no quotation. Wesley reads not slack as not delay, since delay makes a man both unable and unwilling to pay.

Calvin then turns on those who wrest the words to every vow whatever. The Papists would have all kept without exception, since it is written that thou shalt not slack to pay whatever has passed thy lips; but a definition is wanted first, or some account of which God approves. If everything rashly promised had to be performed, it would once have been right to kill sons and daughters and raise altars to idols, and the whole law would fall under that pretext. So a distinction must be drawn, or right and wrong are confounded. Nothing can properly be vowed but what we know pleases him: since obedience is better than sacrifice, nothing is more absurd than each man serving God after his own fancy, and had a Jew vowed a dog it were sacrilege to pay. It may be objected that between the prescribed and the forbidden lies a middle ground of indifferent things. Calvin answers that nothing is to be done without faith, so it must be asked whether a thing agrees with the word; God has left much unforbidden that he will not receive as worship, and a man vowing never to taste meat again would act superstitiously though the abstinence itself were lawful.

The next verse cuts the other way, and Gill marks it: forbearing to vow is no sin. A man was expected to bring freewill offerings proportioned to his ability, of herd or flock or fowl or fine flour — but if he did not vow, no guilt followed. Calvin makes this the aggravation. No necessity compelled the promise, so guilt is doubled in those who chose to sin when silence was open, as Peter told Ananias the field was his own and might have been kept, so that defrauding God of part of the price was sheer hypocrisy. Indirectly God teaches restraint by releasing them: no reason to incur guilt by idly promising what he does not ask. Nothing is wiser than to be sparing of vows, since those who plunge in either repent at once or pay in a servile temper, driven as by force and with disgust, which destroys the grace of the act. The phrase gone out of thy lips is no ceremony, as the Jews too scrupulously insist, but a curb: the tongue outruns the heart, so a vow is complete only when the two agree. Wesley states the residue exactly — free while unmade; once made, a man is no longer free but bound.
24:
The chapter closes with two liberties and two limits. In a neighbour's vineyard a man may eat grapes at his own pleasure, but put none in his vessel; in his standing corn he may pluck the ears with his hand, but move no sickle. Keil states the principle behind both: a passer-by might eat at pleasure to still his hunger, but not carry off a store of grapes or ears, and he observes that the right of hungry travellers to pluck, rub out and eat as they cross a field is still recognised among the Arabs. Gill pictures the vineyard visit — a man invited in to walk, or stepping in as he passes, perhaps on purpose to taste the fruit and quench his thirst; and the cornfield the same, the road often running through standing grain, as when Christ and his disciples went through the corn. He notes that Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan read the second case of a hired workman taking his wages in kind, but prefers the plainer sense, which the example given confirms and which agrees better with what follows. The ears are plucked, rubbed to loose the grain from husk and beard, and eaten to satisfy hunger; what is forbidden is bringing a sickle to cut and carry any of it off, which would be simple injustice. Wesley adds only that eating at pleasure could be allowed in those parts because of the great plenty and fruitfulness of the vines.

Ellicott meets the same rabbinic narrowing on the first clause. Rashi tries to confine both precepts to the labourer gathering vintage or harvest, when vessels are used and sickles employed; but the plain meaning will stand, and our Lord accepts it in the Gospel. The proof is in the objection raised against the disciples, which was not that they plucked their neighbour's corn — nobody disputed that — but that they did it on the Sabbath, plucking counting with the scribes as a kind of harvesting and so unlawful on that day. Clarke draws the moral of both verses together: it was on the permission granted by this law that the disciples plucked the ears, and the statute is a considerate and humane one, no dishonour to the Jewish code.

Calvin knows the restriction to harvest labourers, reporting it from the Chaldee and from the Hebrews generally, but will have none of it. The concession is to all persons, and grants no more licence than humanity demands. His argument is that the words must not be strained but the Lawgiver's intention consulted. God forbids bringing a sickle into another's harvest — very well; then if a man plucked with his bare hands as many ears as he could carry on his shoulders or load upon a horse, is he excused because he used no sickle? Common sense repudiates such gross impudence, so the law plainly has another object: that no one touch even a single ear of another man's crop except for present use. That was the disciples' case, driven by hunger to rub out the corn lest they faint by the way. The grapes fall under the same rule. A man who deliberately breaks into a vineyard and gorges himself there is a thief whatever excuse he offers; and Calvin notes that vineyards were hedged and guarded, so the fruit was never simply exposed to any glutton. What the law permits is that hungry travellers without other food may refresh themselves — liberty to eat their fill, but not on that pretext to stuff themselves, and only until they reach the lodging where bread and wine can be bought. Stretching out a hand to the hanging fruit for present necessity, Calvin concludes, is not to be reckoned theft at all.
